articles.title: Brazil releases the world’s first fossil fuel phaseout roadmap
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The question hanging over international climate talks for years has not really been whether the world would shift away from fossil fuels. It has been whether the countries most responsible for burning them would actually put that transition in writing, with a plan attached. On November 3, Brazil did […]
The post Brazil releases the world’s first fossil fuel phaseout roadmap first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

The question hanging over international climate talks for years has not really been whether the world would shift away from fossil fuels. It has been whether the countries most responsible for burning them would actually put that transition in writing, with a plan attached. On November 3, Brazil did exactly that, releasing what it calls the world’s first global roadmap for phasing out coal, oil and gas.

The document doesn’t bind anyone. It’s voluntary, and it acknowledges upfront that countries will move at different speeds and need different kinds of support. It names the transition as “urgent, inevitable and yet possible” and lays out a three-phase agenda running from 2028 to 2033, during which countries are urged to start drawing up plans and transforming their energy systems. “Countries differ in how fast they can move and in the support they need,” it states, “but every country gains from immediately planning its transition away from fossil fuels.”

Why COP30 ended without naming fossil fuels

The COP30 climate summit, held earlier this year in Belém, ended without final text that explicitly named fossil fuels. Saudi Arabia, Russia, and other major oil producers pushed back against direct language. Fortunately, the Brazilian presidency didn’t treat that as a dead end. Instead, it spent the remaining months of its COP30 term putting together a voluntary framework that any country can use to plan its own phaseout, entirely separate from whatever gets negotiated at a formal summit.

COP30 chief executive Ana Toni framed the roadmap in terms of self-interest as much as obligation. “The transition is inevitable, so start planning now and as soon as possible, because this will be good for your country, for your society, for your economy,” she said. Brazil also released a companion roadmap on halting deforestation by 2030.

A three-phase transition plan, tailored by country

The roadmap doesn’t tell anyone exactly what to do. It says outright that “there is no unique solution for this complex puzzle” and pushes countries to tailor their approach to their own circumstances and starting points. The framing throughout is that the transition is a logistics problem, something to start working on with tools and knowledge that already exist, not a debate to be settled at some future summit.

COP30 president André Corrêa do Lago was blunt about it: “Everyone can start to act now. The agreements already exist. What’s important is to implement them.” The document also points out that current policies still leave the world short of the commitments made at COP28 in Dubai in 2023, when nearly 200 nations agreed to language about “transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems.” Three years later, that language hasn’t moved much. The roadmap is an attempt to change that without waiting on another round of negotiations to get there.

The roadmap’s role at COP31 in Antalya

The COP31 conference opened in Antalya, Turkey, on November 9 with the roadmap on the agenda, though Brazil has been clear it’s not there for renegotiation. “We are not suggesting negotiations,” Corrêa do Lago said. It’s a standing offer.

Turkey and Australia, which are co-steering this year’s talks, have put electrification at the center of COP31’s agenda as a path to cutting emissions. The concern critics have raised is a practical one: the draft text doesn’t specify clean sources, which leaves open the possibility that “electrification” gets used to describe fossil fuel expansion rather than a genuine move to renewables. How that plays out over the two weeks in Antalya will shape what the summit actually delivers.

Climate advocates are pushing for specificity. “The roadmap must not end up as just another report gathering dust on a shelf,” said Fanny Petitbon, a policy analyst at 350.org. “COP31 must be the moment when governments take this work forward, with clear commitments, timelines and the resources to deliver a fair and orderly exit from coal, oil and gas.”

The framing shift that may outlast any summit

The roadmap has no legal teeth. However, what it does have is a particular assumption baked in, namely that the question isn’t whether the fossil fuel transition happens, but how. That’s a different starting point than the one that has dominated climate negotiations for most of the past decade, where the fight was still about whether countries would formally commit to leaving fossil fuels behind at all. Brazil’s document takes that commitment as a given and asks what planning for it looks like. Whether the summits that follow treat it that way remains to be seen, but the document is in the world now, and that changes what any country can point to when it decides to start.

articles.title: Bid to restore rare Atlantic rainforest secures £6m lottery grant
articles.summary: Hubs offering training in conservation work are to be set up in Torridon, Morvern and mid-Argyll.
articles.content:
Almost £6m has been given to a five-year project set up to restore Scotland's rare rainforest.

The award from the National Lottery Heritage Fund will support the creation of three hubs to be located in Torridon, Morvern and mid-Argyll.

Through the Our Rainforest Futures project local people will be given training and work opportunities around habitat restoration, deer management and the removal of invasive species.

About 75,000 acres (30,351ha) of rain-soaked woodlands on the west coast are designated Atlantic rainforest because of the rare oceanic plant life.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant £6m funding award to restore a rare and ecologically important Atlantic rainforest in Scotland, with a clear focus on habitat restoration, invasive species removal, and community training. This project has broad environmental significance and tangible positive impact on conservation and local communities over a five-year period.
articles.personality_title: £6m Lottery Grant to Restore Scotland's Rare Atlantic Rainforest
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scotland is home to a rare type of rainforest called the Atlantic rainforest. This forest covers about 75,000 acres on the west coast and is special because of its unique oceanic plants.

**What happened** – A project called Our Rainforest Futures received almost £6 million from the National Lottery Heritage Fund. The money will be used over five years to create three hubs in Torridon, Morvern, and mid-Argyll. These hubs will train local people in conservation work, including restoring habitats, managing deer, and removing invasive species.

**Impact** – This project will help protect and restore a rare natural environment that is important for many plants and animals. It also gives local people new skills and job opportunities, helping communities connect with nature and support the forest’s health.

**What's next step** – Over the next five years, the hubs will start training sessions and conservation activities. The project aims to improve the forest’s condition and encourage more community involvement in protecting this special area.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A £6 million grant is funding a five-year plan to restore Scotland’s rare Atlantic rainforest while training local people to care for it.

articles.title: Biotech innovations are an opportunity to limit climate change
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03621-yAgricultural biotechnology once found itself in opposition to environmental science. Now it could reduce the impact of food systems on global warming and biodiversity loss.
articles.content:
Agricultural biotechnology once found itself in opposition to environmental science. Now it could reduce the impact of food systems on global warming and biodiversity loss.

Climate change is affecting many types of crop, including these unusually small potatoes.Credit: John Thys/AFP/Getty

Policymakers at the United Nations COP31 climate conference that started this week in Antalya, Turkey, will know that the UN Environment Programme has confirmed that global warming will exceed the limit of 1.5 °C above pre-industrial temperatures agreed in 2015 in Paris. This meeting comes hot on the heels of the UN COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia, which affirmed yet again that the world is also in the middle of a biodiversity crisis. Progress in each case, whether preventing dangerous climate change or stemming biodiversity loss, is too slow. But researchers across scientific disciplines are now arguing that advances in biotechnology could provide solutions1. Methods such as gene editing and germplasm mining — the analysis of huge libraries of plant-genome sequences to find useful traits for crop improvement — can now be used to tackle global warming and protect nature, scientists write in a climate-themed issue of Nature Biotechnology.

The seeds of resilience

There was a time — not that long ago — when many considered biotechnologies a threat to the environment. But as the special issue shows, a shift is under way. Now, the field offers strategies for protecting both climate and biodiversity from the many damaging effects of industrial agriculture.

To feed a growing global population, between 2015 and 2024, the amount of cultivated land grew by roughly eight million hectares a year1. Yet, if the greenhouse-gas emissions, and thus global warming, this expansion causes is to be avoided, the world must work out how to produce enough food within its current agricultural footprint. Land clearance and land-use change contributes up to five billion tonnes of carbon annually — and is a major cause of biodiversity loss. Here, biotech solutions have some of the greatest potential, for example, by helping to increase crop yields and to protect plants from heat, drought and disease.

How biotechnology can mitigate climate change by curbing the global land squeeze

Of 77 such technologies with applications in agriculture, aquaculture and other sectors, many are ready for large-scale testing in the field, propose bioengineers Shekhar Mishra, Lauren Lui and Adam Arkin at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in California in a Perspective article2. Argentina, China and the United States have given the green light to engineered drought-tolerant crops.

Rice farming produces around 9% of human-caused emissions of the greenhouse gas methane. Now, researchers have found a way to slash these emissions, write agronomist Yunkai Jin at Hunan Agricultural University in Changsha, China, and his colleagues in a Comment article3.

But technological readiness isn’t enough: governments, regulators and the public need to be ready, too4. Readers might have a sense of déjà vu: in the 1990s, advances in biotechnology promised a revolution in food and agriculture — which subsequently stalled. The ambition was to genetically modify crops or engineer them in other ways so that they could tolerate herbicides, resist insects and fight viruses. But, at the time, many scientists, governments and corporations promoting the technology gave insufficient attention to several issues.

Deployability of biotechnologies for environmentally resilient agriculture

One concern was public anxiety about the idea of eating food produced using transgenic technologies — crops modified by inserting a gene from another plant species or other organism. Another issue was that risks to the environment and to human health had not been studied sufficiently. A third problem was that multinational companies dominated both the research and the development of these technologies, creating fears that the rise of agricultural biotechnology would put many small family farms out of business.

Environmental groups found common cause with consumer organizations. Together, they urged governments to enact strict regulations. In the European Union, for example, risks to human health and the environment needed to be assessed before technologies producing genetically modified organisms could be commercialized. Although this was necessary, it slowed down advances in low- and middle-income countries, because any nation intending to export produce to the EU would have to prove that it was not genetically modified.

All change

Since then, at least two things have changed, increasing optimism about the use of biotechnology to help the planet. The discovery of gene editing — in which an organism’s genes are modified precisely to produce specific traits — has proved transformational for agriculture. The method is being developed cautiously and is regulated in a more nuanced way than were conventional technologies that produce genetically modified crops. In June, the EU amended its regulations on genetic modification and now permits the cultivation of some gene-edited crops.

Low-methane rice is near — the world should deploy it

A second development is that catastrophic events such as heatwaves and floods have meant that climate change and the planet’s protection have become mainstream concerns across science and society, not just for environmental research. In a way, we all need to be environmentalists now, and this provides a rationale for governments to reconsider adopting biotech solutions with appropriate safeguards in place.

Advances in biotechnology that limit land use should be deployed to slow down the rise in global temperatures and biodiversity loss. This will require a partnership between the private sector, scientists, conservationists and farmers. High-yielding crops produced using industrial agriculture have helped to feed the world but have also had a devastating effect on biodiversity. Organic agriculture is more sustainable but requires extra land, because its yields tend to be lower than those from industrial methods. Providing they are implemented wisely, safely and ethically, biotechnologies could contribute to innovative farming methods that offer the best of both worlds.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on significant advances in agricultural biotechnology that have the potential to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, limit land use expansion, and protect biodiversity, addressing major global environmental challenges. It highlights broad, meaningful impacts for global food systems and climate change mitigation, with detailed context on technological readiness, regulatory shifts, and the need for multi-sector collaboration.
articles.personality_title: New biotech tools offer ways to reduce farming’s impact on climate and nature
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Climate change and loss of biodiversity are big problems linked to how we grow food. Expanding farmland causes more greenhouse gases and harms natural habitats. Scientists and policymakers are looking for new ways to produce enough food without hurting the planet.

Some countries, like the US, China, and Argentina, have approved drought-resistant crops. Scientists have also found ways to reduce methane emissions from rice farming, which is important because rice farming produces a lot of greenhouse gases.

**Impact** – This is important because it shows that biotechnology can help fight climate change and protect wildlife by making farming more efficient on the same amount of land. This means less need to clear forests or other natural areas for farming, which lowers carbon emissions and saves habitats. New gene editing methods are safer and more accepted now than older genetic modification techniques, making it easier to use these tools.

Rules are changing, like in the European Union, where some gene-edited crops are now allowed. The next steps will include testing these crops more widely and finding ways to use them safely and fairly around the world.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New gene editing and biotech methods can help grow more food with less harm to the climate and nature, offering promising tools to meet future challenges in farming.

articles.title: Daily briefing: Where academic freedom is declining — and where it’s on the rise
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03664-1Academic freedom is deteriorating globally, but has soared in a few countries in recent years. Plus, testimony from a member of a year-long simulated Mars mission and how key fungal networks could save Mongolia’s iconic grasslands.
articles.content:
Academic freedom is deteriorating globally, but has soared in a few countries in recent years. Plus, testimony from a member of a year-long simulated Mars mission and how key fungal networks could save Mongolia’s iconic grasslands.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

Matthew Montgomery, the science officer of a simulated Mars mission organized by NASA, takes part in a ‘Martian’ geology project.Credit: NASA

Engineer Matthew Montgomery was one of a four-person crew who spent more than a year in a 158-square-metre, 3D-printed habitat for a simulated mission on the red planet. The hardware-engineering design consultant (and co-owner of a film production company) took charge of the hydroponic garden and participated in simulated ‘Marswalks’ wearing a protective suit. As well as dealing with a realistic 13–22 minute delay in their connection with mission control, the crew experienced a total communication blackout for two weeks.

Nature | 7 min read

News

A new artificial-intelligence tool can identify an individual bird by its song, and can be used to track that bird’s movements over time. The system provides a less invasive way to monitor birds than using physical tags. Researchers tested the model on recordings of male ovenbirds (Seiurus aurocapilla) — a species that sings individually unique songs — from more than 100 locations, and found that it could match songs to specific birds with up to 96% accuracy. “This is almost a holy grail,” says biologist Scott Sillett.

Science | 4 min read

Reference: Nature Methods papers

US$200 The amount that preprint platform XSci pays referees for a quick-turnaround peer review. Authors pay up to $399 for a round of review. (Nature | 10 min read)

Protecting key underground fungal networks in Mongolia could help to preserve biodiversity, boost climate resilience and revive iconic grasslands across the country, say researchers. In September, evolutionary biologist Toby Kiers and her team announced that they had found more than 500 types of fungus in networks across Mongolia, 90% of which were new to science. Mycologist Burenjargal Otgonsuren hopes that leveraging these networks could help to restore the swathes of degraded land in Mongolia — and preserve the 3,000-year-old way of life practiced by Mongolia’s 230,000 nomadic herding families.

By studying people who show no signs of neurodegeneration well into older age, scientists have identified several gene variants that could help to protect against dementia. These protective variants seem to defend the brain against the toxic clusters of proteins that cause Alzheimer’s — mechanisms that scientists now hope to exploit. “Nature has already done the experiment for us: certain gene variants protect us from Alzheimer’s,” says neuroscientist Guojun Bu. “Learning how they do this could guide us to new therapies.”

Biomining strategies — those that use microorganisms to extract metals — could provide a more sustainable alternative to conventional technologies, which are struggling to keep up with soaring demand for critical minerals, argue a group of biotechnology and mining researchers. These methods can also extract metals from discarded electronics, reducing the need for virgin ores. For biomining methods to reach their potential, researchers must work with governments and industry to establish a pathway through which these technologies can be deployed at scale, the authors write.

Mycologist Burenjargal Otgonsuren believes protecting and using these fungal networks can help restore damaged lands and support the herding communities.

articles.personality_title_fr: De nouvelles découvertes fongiques en Mongolie pour restaurer les prairies et soutenir la vie nomade

articles.personality_title_es: Nuevos descubrimientos de hongos en Mongolia ofrecen esperanza para restaurar pastizales y la vida nómada
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los vastos pastizales de Mongolia son importantes para la naturaleza y para las 230,000 familias que viven como pastores nómadas. Sin embargo, muchas áreas de estos pastizales han sufrido daños con el tiempo, poniendo en riesgo tanto el medio ambiente como las formas tradicionales de vida.

**Qué pasó** – Científicos liderados por la bióloga evolutiva Toby Kiers encontraron más de 500 tipos de hongos subterráneos en los suelos de Mongolia, de los cuales el 90 % son nuevos para la ciencia. Estos hongos forman redes que son clave para la salud de los pastizales. La micóloga Burenjargal Otgonsuren cree que proteger y aprovechar estas redes fúngicas puede ayudar a restaurar las tierras dañadas y apoyar a las comunidades de pastores.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento es importante porque estos hongos ayudan a las plantas a crecer y sobrevivir en condiciones difíciles. Al comprender y proteger los hongos, los científicos pueden mejorar la salud de los pastizales, lo que a su vez apoya la biodiversidad y el modo de vida nómada. Esto ofrece una forma natural de combatir la degradación del suelo sin usar químicos o maquinaria pesada.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores esperan colaborar con las comunidades locales y gobiernos para aplicar este conocimiento en la restauración de los pastizales de Mongolia. Estudiarán cómo proteger mejor los hongos y usarlos para devolver el equilibrio natural a la tierra. El éxito podría inspirar esfuerzos similares en otras regiones.

**Resumen en una frase** – Científicos han descubierto nuevas redes de hongos en Mongolia que podrían ayudar a sanar pastizales dañados y apoyar a los pastores nómadas del país.
